title: Zero-Trust Egress Gateway — workshop notes and POC checklist
content:
Context:
This is a working capture from the 2024-10-03 SE workshop on a zero‑trust egress gateway pattern for Private deployments (VPC/on‑prem). Goal: produce a small POC plan customers can run to validate secure outbound connectivity without creating broad internet NAT holes or relying on customer-managed bastions.

High-level problem statement:
- Customers want to keep inference traffic tightly controlled when we run in their VPCs or on their premises.
- Hard requirements we repeatedly hear: least-privilege egress, audit trails, TLS-authenticated service egress, no wide-open NATs, simple DNS handoff, and predictable failover for model updates.

Key constraints / assumptions for POC:
- Target cloud: AWS (notes for GCP/Azure below).
- We assume customer can accept a small number of VPC endpoint interfaces / proxy subnets, and a single outbound IP pool for allowlisting by SaaS partners.
- We avoid introducing inbound firewall rules into customer subnets.
- KMS/HSM: keys are customer-managed where required.

Architecture sketch (ASCII):

  [Customer VPC]                            [Redwood Control Plane / Registry]
  +----------+    (1) request to model API   +-----------------------------+
  | Private  |-------------------------------->  HTTPS  (mTLS optional)  |
  | Subnets  |                                 |  (hosted endpoints)     |
  | (SE hosts)|                                +-----------------------------+
  |          |
  |  [Egress Gateway]  <--(2) egress tunnel / proxy--->  [Outbound Proxy fleet]
  |  - ENI in svc-subnet
  |  - IP allowlist for vendors
  +----------+

Design components and options:
1) Egress Gateway (customer-side) — options:
   A. Containerized Envoy sidecar in a dedicated svc-subnet (recommended for POC)
      - Pros: fine-grained routing, TLS origination, and policy enforcement (RBAC based on client certs).
      - Cons: requires deployment orchestration + health checks.

   B. Managed NAT with Source IP tagging + proxy (simpler but less auditable)
      - Pros: lower ops surface.
      - Cons: source IPs reveal limited identity; can't do mTLS per-service.

   C. AWS Gateway Load Balancer + partner virtual appliance (for customers with appliance requirements)

2) DNS split-horizon + handoff strategy:
   - Customer DNS (Route53 private hosted zones) must resolve redwood-internal.* to the ENI IPs in the svc-subnet.
   - For SaaS egress (calling external vendor HTTP APIs), use explicit prefix list and outbound-proxy FQDNs.
   - Avoid wildcard forwarding to public DNS; do explicit forward rules for vendor domains to reduce leakage.

3) Authentication and identity:
   - Prefer mTLS between egress gateway and Redwood outbound proxy (client cert burned into gateway via KMS-backed secret).
   - For host identity inside VPC, use short-lived IAM roles (IRSA for EKS) to fetch certs/keys from Secrets Manager.

4) Observability & audit:
   - Wire logs from Envoy to customer CloudWatch/Datadog; include request_id (generated at request ingress) and app principal.
   - Trace: add X-RW-Trace header and sample 1% of requests for perf profiles.

5) Failover policies:
   - Local fail-open vs remote fallback: POC uses automatic failover to a regional Redwood outbound pool, only after local gateway health checks fail for N=3 intervals.
   - Circuit breaker: per-vendor circuit with exponential backoff to avoid cascading failures during vendor slowdowns.

AWS-specific nitty-gritty (POC checklist items):
- Subnet plan: create a dedicated svc-subnet in each AZ for egress gateway ENIs.
- Route table tweaks: route 0.0.0.0/0 -> NAT or GWLB depending on option chosen.
- Interface endpoints: prefer S3/SecretsManager Gateway endpoints where cert fetching is needed (S3 gateway endpoint is free, interface endpoints cost money).
- Security groups: tighten SGs to only allow outbound to Redwood outbound proxies (by CIDR or prefix list).
- Prefix lists: if customer needs vendor allowlisting, coordinate to exchange prefix list IDs.

GCP/Azure notes (short):
- GCP: use Private Service Connect for interface proxies; Cloud NAT for non-proxy traffic.
- Azure: use Service Endpoint / Private Link and NAT Gateway with forced tunneling where needed.

POC implementation plan (sprint-sized):
- Day 0: Kickoff, confirm customer constraints (e.g., allowed outbound IPs, required vendors), produce IP/FQDN allowlist. (Owner: Aisha)
- Day 1–3: Provision svc-subnet + small EKS/ECS task running Envoy-based gateway (templates in infra repo). (Owner: Marco)
- Day 4: Configure Route53 private hosted zone and conditional forwarders; set up Secrets Manager + KMS for certs. (Owner: Riley)
- Day 5: Wire up mTLS between gateway and Redwood outbound proxy; small smoke tests. (Owner: Priya)
- Day 6–7: Run traffic, capture logs/traces, tweak circuit breakers and DNS TTLs. Produce evaluation checklist. (Owner: Samir)

POC checklist (quick):
- [ ] svc-subnet created in each AZ
- [ ] Envoy gateway deployed (health checks green)
- [ ] KMS key + runtime secret rotation working
- [ ] Route53 entries for redwood-internal.* pointing to ENI IPs
- [ ] Security groups restricted to outbound proxies/prefix list
- [ ] Prefix list exchange complete with vendor allowlists
- [ ] mTLS end-to-end verified with cert rotation
- [ ] Traces/logs flowing to customer observability
- [ ] Failure mode tested (gateway shutdown -> failover to regional pool)

Open questions / risks discovered in workshop:
- Cert provisioning cadence: who rotates client cert used by envoys? (Ops vs customer)
- Large customer networks: will customers accept adding ENIs and route table rules? Need procurement checklist.
- Edge case: third-party APIs that validate via source IP and do not support TLS client certs — mapping strategy? (Use outbound IP allowlist + vendor coordination).
- Audit logging compliance: some regulated customers need logs kept on their side for 7+ years; we need a retention plan.

Decisions / constraints to propose in RFC:
- Use mTLS by default for POC where customer can provide KMS-managed secrets.
- Default gateway pattern = Envoy in svc-subnet with per-tenant prefix list controls.
- No inbound port openings to customer subnets; all control plane egress initiated from our agents.

Short list of follow-ups (action items):
- Aisha: Draft customer preflight checklist for networking team (due 2024-10-10).
- Marco: Add Terraform module skeleton for svc-subnet + envoy autoscaling group (PR: infra-provisioning).
- Riley: Create a small demo script that rotates a client cert and verifies Envoy picks it up without restart.
- Priya: Coordinate with Ops to produce runbook for failover testing.

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep DNS TTLs low (30s–120s) during POC so we can flip endpoints quickly.
- Watch out for AWS per-account ENI limits in large-scale multi-tenant POCs.
- If a customer uses on-prem K8s, adapt to daemonset envoy instead of EKS task.

Resources / references:
- internal: confluence/EGRESS Gateway Design RFC (see linked_artifacts)
- infra repo PR with envoy config snippet: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra-provisioning/pull/198
- example cert rotation pattern: https://github.com/hashicorp/vault-guides/tree/main/k8s-auth

Session notes (freeform):
- Customer X is very strict about not adding NAT; they will accept the svc-subnet ENI pattern if we can guarantee no ephemeral SSH ingress.
- Customer Y wants vendor allowlisting by FQDN only (no IPs). We need to confirm vendor support for SNI-based allowlisting.
- Consider a small script we can give customers to validate that only permitted outbound hostnames resolve via private DNS (dig + curl smoke checks).

End of doc — this is a living workshop capture. Update status when RFC decision made.
